title: SECRET NOFO
summary: A declassification-release notice for the Hughes Glomar Explorer (AZORIAN) project. It states that most details remain classified despite 1975 media coverage. Litigation (California tax, FOIA, patent claims) has led the U.S. Government to acknowledge CIA sponsorship for intelligence collection, participation of Hughes Tool Company, Summa Corporation, and Global Marine, and 1975 CIA efforts to dissuade media reports. All other details stay classified, including mission purpose, success, operations, contractors, technology, and funding. The article is published at SECRET NOFORN level, with most project details still restricted.

title: PROJECT AZORIAN:

nodes.title: PROJECT AZORIAN: (intro)
nodes.summary: Project AZORIAN, the CIA operation using the Hughes Glomar Explorer to recover a lost Soviet G-II submarine from 16,500 feet in the Pacific (lost March 1968, recovery 1974). Covers the project's scale, technical complexity, cost, and risks; high-level officials' knowledge and differing opinions on proceeding; the February 1975 Los Angeles Times leak after a June 1974 Summa Corporation break-in; and Jack Anderson's March 1975 media disclosure.

nodes.title: It
Project Origin
nodes.summary: Describes the origin of the Glomar project (code-named AZORIAN, not JENNIFER): a 1968 Soviet G-II-class diesel ballistic missile submarine sank 1,560 miles northwest of Hawaii, prompting a fruitless two-month Soviet search. DoD and CIA officials sought to recover submarine components for Soviet strategic intelligence. Covers a document-leak risk involving Howard Hughes, Los Angeles Times disclosure, DCI Colby's containment efforts, and Anderson's decision to publish. Notes later articles will cover the AZORIAN/MATADOR cover program.

nodes.title: Organizing for Recovery
nodes.summary: Describes CIA and Department of Defense efforts in 1968-1969 to recover components of the sunken G-II submarine (Project AZORIAN). Covers Packard's April 1969 letter to Helms, designation of coordinators, the 8 August 1969 ExCom approval and President Nixon's notification, the 19 August 1969 organizational agreement, the JENNIFER security system and compartmentation, the extreme need-to-know security, and the Special Projects Staff task force led by John Parangosky with Zellmer as deputy.

nodes.title: Development of Engineering Concept
nodes.summary: Parangosky assembled a small engineering task force in a 'think tank' room to design a concept for recovering a Soviet submarine. Three security-cleared contractors assisted with structures, naval architecture, and sensors. Criteria were technical and operational feasibility, timely fielding for an early recovery, and reasonable cost. No country had ever raised an object of such size and weight from that depth.

nodes.title: l. Early Concepts
nodes.summary: Covers three early lift concepts for raising a submarine hull section from the seabed: (a) total brute-force direct lift using the Rosenberg Winch with wire ropes rated for about 2,000-2,200 long tons, with a drill string rejected as undeployable; (b) trade ballast/buoyancy, where buoyant material is carried down, ballast is dropped on the bottom, and positive buoyancy lifts the target; (c) at-depth buoyancy generation via electrolysis, cryogenic gases, hydrazine decomposition, or reactive metals/hydrides (sodium, lithium, lithium hydride) producing gas.

nodes.title: 4. Engineering Concept Selected
nodes.summary: Covers the engineering concept selection for a recovery mission: by late July 1970 the heavy-lift concept was favored and got full attention, with formal authorization to focus studies on it granted at a 11 September 1970 Pentagon briefing. Also mentions a deep-ocean mining cover story developed to explain project activities, especially at-sea operations. The text is fragmentary and partly garbled.

nodes.title: Executive Committee Approval
nodes.summary: At the 30 October 1970 Executive Committee meeting, the target recovery concept was discussed. A dead-lift (brute force) method would lift the estimated 1,750-ton object from 16,500 feet using heavy-lifting equipment on a large surface ship (Glomar Explorer). A deep-sea mining venture serves as cover story, with a mining device mated to the ship's center well and a submersible dry dock planned. Major technical risk areas were identified.

Describes the Project AZORIAN (Glomar) effort to recover a sunken 1968 Soviet G-II submarine 1,560 miles northwest of Hawaii, including the Hughes leak risk, LA Times disclosure, and Anderson's publication decision. Covers CIA/DoD organizing in 1968-69, the JENNIFER security compartmentation, and the Parangosky task force. Details engineering lift concepts (brute-force, buoyancy trade, at-depth gas generation), selection of heavy-lift in 1970, the deep-ocean mining cover story, and the 30 October 1970 Executive Committee approval with its technical risks.

nodes.title: They were characterized as being
nodes.summary: Describes the Glomar/AZORIAN project: the ship was state-of-the-art but needed strengthening for heavy weights and pressures; its control system was seen as a risk but proven feasible by the Glomar Challenger. Simulation testing was planned, and early analyses found no insurmountable problems. Success odds were estimated near 10% initially, rising to about 90% before the mission. Officials debated the target's value, whether material would be recoverable in usable condition, and funding. Packard directed proceeding, with planning and funding sources to be identified. Cost rose due to extended testing and cover/admin expenses, while hardware costs changed little.

nodes.title: The Crucial 4 August ExCom Meeting
key_items: Early Political Feasibility Evaluation by 40 Committee
nodes.summary: Covers the crucial 4 August 1971 ExCom meeting on the AZORIAN (Glomar) project, where cost growth, budget strain, high intelligence value, and operational risks were debated, and Packard allowed continuation with cost review and alternatives. Describes subsequent cost increases, design and construction progress (ship keel laid, pipe string, subsystems, data processing), and 1972 managerial views on delays and expenses. Details the 40 Committee political feasibility review and conflicting memos from Rush, Zumwalt, Hall, de Poix, Moorer, and Helms, with Rush ultimately favoring termination due to political and technical risks. Ends by noting Rush's creation of a review panel under Hall to examine costs and termination savings.

summary: Project AZORIAN: CIA operation using the Hughes Glomar Explorer to recover a sunken 1968 Soviet G-II submarine at 16,500 feet, 1,560 miles northwest of Hawaii (recovered 1974). Covers scale, technical lift concepts, cost, odds of success, security compartmentation, the deep-ocean mining cover story, 1970 ExCom approval, the June 1974 Summa break-in, the February 1975 LA Times leak, Anderson's March 1975 disclosure, the 1971 ExCom cost debate, 40 Committee review, and Rush's termination recommendation and review panel.

title: SEGRE

nodes.title: The Glomar Story
AZORIAN Review Panel findings on Glomar program status and risks
key_items: program office planning the target date.
nodes.summary: The AZORIAN Review Panel, convened by Helms and Rush and reporting 11 December 1972, found the program well managed with key phases on schedule, but flagged high technical risk from state-of-the-art developments such as large forgings, new pipe metallurgy, and an untestable lifting apparatus. It concluded termination savings depend on cover and market competitiveness, cost growth was creditable (about 6% since December 1971), and further growth was likely during testing. Engineering unknowns were the greatest uncertainty.

nodes.title: The 40 Committee Decision to Proceed
The 40 Committee Decision to Proceed (intro)
Construction and Delivery of HGE
nodes.summary: Covers the 11 December 1972 presidential decision to continue the AZORIAN (Glomar) project under 40 Committee oversight, after a detailed program review, and the project's praise for interagency cooperation. Describes the Hughes Glomar Explorer's construction: GMI's 1971 announcement, the 4 November 1972 launch at Sun Shipbuilding, well-gate guide installation, and planned mid-1973 builders' trials and Coast Guard/ABS certification. Trials are grouped into general, standard, and unconventional ship tests.

nodes.title: Summary of Trials and Trial Data-~Builder’s Trials
nodes.summary: Builder's trials of the HGE were conducted 12-14 April (from Sun Shipyard, Chester, Pa.) in the Atlantic about 75 nautical miles southeast of Delaware Bay, with 203 people aboard including Sun Ship, Global Marine, Special Project Staff, ABS and Coast Guard representatives. Sun Ship personnel operated the ship in good weather; all tests succeeded, handling was rated excellent, and some major and minor discrepancies were found for correction before delivery. Trials ended with thruster tests, the ship returned to Chester on 15 April, and deficiencies were corrected ahead of East Coast trials scheduled for July 1978.

nodes.title: East Coast Trials, July-August 1973
nodes.summary: Covers the East Coast trials of the Hughes Glomar Explorer, July-August 1973: retesting basic marine systems and testing heavy lift, docking legs, heave compensator, gimbal platform, and pipe-handling at sea. Curtis Crooke was test director, with reviewers signing off each test. Departure from Sun Shipyard on 24 July, passage under the Delaware Memorial Bridge (derrick top removed and reinstalled by crane), deep-water tests (ASK, pipe-handling, gimbal) northwest of Bermuda, then Bermuda crew change before the transit to Long Beach.

nodes.title: Results of East Coast Trials
nodes.summary: Summarizes East Coast trial results for a ship (HGE): basic ship systems performed well except some deficiencies; hull sound; major structures (well gates, A-frame, gimbal platform, derrick, docking legs) structurally sound with no major rework needed. Mining equipment mostly operated as designed with several serious and many minor deficiencies. Corrective tasks planned: 40 before leaving Bermuda, 136 during transit to Long Beach, 245 during West Coast mobilization.

nodes.title: East-West Transit, 11 August-30 September 1973
nodes.summary: Describes the Hughes Glomar Explorer's 1973 East-West transit from Bermuda to Valparaiso, Chile. Covers the 12,700-mile route (the beam too wide for the Panama Canal), the 96-person crew, Chilean pilots through the Strait of Magellan, weather, contingency plans amid Chilean unrest, the 6 September Strait transit, and arrival at Valparaiso on 12 September just as the 11 September coup occurred.

nodes.title: The Glomar Explorer's Magellan Strait Transits, 1973 and 1978
key_items: Bermuda to Entrance, Magellan Strait, 11 August-5 September 1973
nodes.summary: Covers the HGE's 1973 Bermuda-to-Entrance leg through Magellan Strait (11 Aug-5 Sep): excellent weather, one brief storm with 50-60 knot winds, good handling, morale, and crew and galley praised. Late-August Chilean unrest prompted contingency plans for pilot unavailability or interference, with alternatives: standing off, rounding Cape Horn, or sailing around South Africa. Also covers the 5-6 September 1978 transit: Chilean pilots embarked, a cold front with 45-50 knot winds slowed progress, and the ship entered the Pacific around 1500 on 6 September.

nodes.title: Strait of Magellan to Valparaiso, Chile, 6-13 September 1973
nodes.summary: Describes the HGE ship's Pacific passage from the Strait of Magellan to Valparaiso, Chile (6-13 September 1973): heavy weather forcing a brief heave-to, uneventful remainder, and crew preparing parts lists for Global Marine. It covers the ship's arrival on 12 September during the military coup, pilots and Chilean naval formalities, and the Global Marine representative Tom Williams's efforts to bring in seven technicians and supplies amid curfew and confusion. The ship sailed for Long Beach on 13 September with no unfavorable incidents.

nodes.title: Valparaiso, Chile, to Long Beach, California, 13-30 September 1973
nodes.summary: Report on the HGE ship's east-west transit leg from Valparaiso, Chile to Long Beach, California (13-30 September 1973) for the AZORIAN program. The voyage was incident-free, with good weather apart from two tropical storms that were avoided. 21 scheduled jobs went unfinished for lack of time. The heavy-lift team boarded at Valparaiso and progressed well. The ship arrived and tied up at Pier E on 30 September, with relief crew boarding the next day. Transit covered 12,745 nm in 50 days 7.5 hours (avg 10.8 knots), consuming 20,643 barrels of fuel (68 gallons per mile).

nodes.title: Mobilization for Mission, October 1973-January 1974
nodes.summary: Describes the mobilization period (October 1973 to January 1974) for the Glomar Explorer mission after its East-West transit and arrival at Long Beach on 30 September. The fitting-out phase, originally planned at about 51 days, ran roughly twice as long to convert the ship from overt to covert configuration. Mission team training ran aboard ship as vans were installed. The crew was set at 178, the lifeboat-capacity maximum, and the mobilization produced a cohesive team. Key roles were listed, and the Mission Director held senior command authority over the ship's captain. The shipboard team closely matched the 1971-1972 plans when the ship sailed in June 1974.

nodes.title: Conversion of the HGE From “White” to “Black”
nodes.summary: Describes conversion of the HGE ship from 'white' (innocuous mining prototype appearance, July 1973 onward, east coast trials and transit around South America to the west coast) to 'black' during mobilization. Covers installing 24 mission vans (8'x8'x20') for recovery and intelligence exploitation, including cleaning, decontamination, paper processing, drying, darkroom, waste handling, dress-out rooms, and packing facilities. Also covers open commercial radio communications via Global Marine and RCA KPH, and weather reporting to Fleet Numerical Weather Central.

nodes.summary:

capability for reception of

nodes.title: Manning
nodes.summary: Covers the Glomar Explorer (HGE) mobilization at Pier E, Long Beach, in late 1973 to early 1974. Labor disputes with MEBA picketing escalated, harassing the crew and halting deliveries. Combined with engineering problems and the holiday period, this delayed sea trials until mid-January 1974. The ship moved to an outer anchorage for the pipe-handling demonstration. Morale concerns led to a crew morale boost. The mission needed a July to mid-September weather window, with a late-June readiness deadline. Soviet ships docked nearby but showed no evidence of learning the true mission, crediting security and cover.

Section on the 40 Committee's decision to proceed with the AZORIAN (Glomar) project: the 11 Dec 1972 presidential approval after program review, and construction of the Hughes Glomar Explorer (HGE). Covers builder's trials (April 1973), East Coast trials (July-August 1973), trial results and corrective tasks, the 1973 East-West transit via Magellan Strait to Valparaiso (coup coincident with arrival), the leg to Long Beach, and conversion from 'white' to 'black' configuration with mission vans, weather facilities, and mobilization/manning issues including labor disputes.

nodes.title: First West Coast Trials, 11 January-23 January 1974
nodes.summary: Covers the first West Coast sea trials of the Glomar Explorer (HGE), January 11-23, 1974: departure from Pier E, the test site about 160 miles WSW of Long Beach, and the MEBA union picket issue. The trials verified the pipe-handling system and crew readiness, and a practice pipe run and five days at anchorage revealed PHS reliability problems. The ship reached the site on January 19 and deployed transponders and a wave-rider buoy. Weather delayed flooding the well. On January 23 an aft well-gate machinery casualty in heavy surges ended the trials. Repairs took 13-15 days by divers, with a small seal leak accepted. The HMB-1 barge's Catalina arrival and press coverage are also noted.

Covers the 40 Committee's 11 Dec 1972 approval of the AZORIAN (Glomar) project and construction of the Hughes Glomar Explorer: builder's trials (April 1973), East Coast trials (July-August 1973) and corrective tasks, the 1973 transit via Magellan Strait to Valparaiso (coup at arrival), the leg to Long Beach, and conversion to 'black' configuration with mission vans, weather facilities, and manning/labor disputes. Also covers West Coast trials (11-23 Jan 1974): pipe-handling verification, PHS reliability problems, transponder and buoy deployment, weather delays, and an aft well-gate casualty with divers' repairs.

nodes.title: Second West Coast ‘Trials 15 February-2 March 1974
Second West Coast ‘Trials 15 February-2 March 1974 (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers the Glomar Explorer's Second West Coast trials (15 Feb-2 Mar 1974): Mission Director selection, well-gate repairs and tests, GMI VP Curtis Crooke aboard, performance criteria for pipe-handling and heavy-lift systems, 40 doubles deployed, sensor/control repairs, the 65 nm offshore move to avoid California inventory tax, return to Long Beach Pier E, and preparation for Integrated Systems Tests starting 28 March 1974 at a shallower 2,600-foot site near Catalina.

nodes.title: A torquer casualty handling problems which
A torquer casualty handling problems which (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes a torquer casualty and in-port repairs, then Control Center crew training success and morale boost. Testing was completed at 2,400 ft, waiving a 12,000 ft deep test, to keep a June 1974 recovery departure. Notes the system's unprecedented size and complexity, one-time-operation design, and reliance on crew workarounds. Testing ended 12 May 1974; the ship returned to Long Beach for a 28–30 day refit before mid-June departure.

nodes.title: Final Approval in Washington
nodes.summary: Describes Project AZORIAN, a planned mission to recover a sunken Soviet submarine. In May 1974 the US Intelligence Board reaffirmed that no developments diminish its unique intelligence value. Successful recovery would yield nuclear warheads, SS-N-5 missile data, documents giving insight into Soviet command and control and strategic attack doctrine, information available from no other source. The 40 Committee discussed it on 5 June, and President Nixon approved on 7 June, barring recovery before his 27 June-3 July Soviet visit.

nodes.title: AZORIAN Mission Recovery, 20 June-16 August 1974
nodes.summary: Chronicles the AZORIAN (Glomar Explorer) recovery mission, June–August 1974: a cover-story acceptance ceremony at Long Beach, transit to the northwest Pacific, and arrival on 4 July. Covers transponder and buoy deployment, pipe-handling tests, weather delays (Typhoon/Gilda, tropical storm Harriet), cracked docking legs repaired, a medical rescue of a Bel Hudson crewman, and the Soviet ship Chazhma's close approaches and radio exchange. Also describes Soviet tug SB-10 surveillance, heavy-lift equipment failures, sonar location and video identification of the submarine wreck, and crew morale.

nodes.title: Lift-off
nodes.summary: Describes the Glomar Explorer's SB-10 recovery operation around 1-3 August: lift-off of the pipe, recovery under way by 2200 on 1 August, and the SB-10 circling the ship amid unidentified radar contacts. On 2 August, pipe lifting went well, with 274 doubles (16,440 feet) deployed and coming up. A cover story was broadcast in the clear on 3 August claiming a collision with a silt-covered outcrop, to justify a request to enter Midway for repairs. The text also covers persistent heavy-lift hydraulic pump problems, bypassed fail-safe circuitry, praise for operators, and the crew's near-aborts, and says the team stayed determined.

Covers the torquer casualty and in-port repairs, Control Center crew training and morale, and testing at 2,400 ft (waiving a 12,000 ft test) to meet a June 1974 departure; testing ended 12 May 1974 with a return to Long Beach for refit. Describes Project AZORIAN, approved by President Nixon on 7 June 1974 after 40 Committee review, to recover a sunken Soviet submarine for warheads, SS-N-5 data, and command-and-control documents. Narrates the Glomar Explorer recovery mission (June-August 1974): transit, weather delays, cracked docking legs, a medical rescue, Soviet ship and tug surveillance, equipment failures, sonar/video identification of the wreck, the pipe lift-off with cover story, hydraulic pump problems, and crew morale.

Covers the Glomar Explorer's Second West Coast trials (15 Feb-2 Mar 1974): well-gate repairs, GMI VP aboard, pipe-handling and heavy-lift tests, sensor/control repairs, a 65 nm offshore move to avoid California inventory tax, and return to Long Beach. Then torquer casualty repairs, crew training, 2,400 ft testing ending 12 May 1974, and refit. Describes Project AZORIAN, approved by Nixon 7 June 1974, to recover a sunken Soviet submarine's warheads and documents. Narrates the June-August 1974 recovery: weather delays, cracked docking legs, a medical rescue, Soviet surveillance, equipment failures, wreck identification, pipe lift-off under a cover story, hydraulic problems, and crew morale.

nodes.title: [The SB-10 continued close surveillance. During
nodes.summary: Describes the Glomar Explorer (HGE) operation in August 1978 (AZORIAN): the SB-10 Soviet vessel conducted 18 days 16 hours of close surveillance, including radio exchanges with the tanker Bangkok, a Summa commercial message about repairing the nodule collector vehicle, maneuvers and a whistle-signaled departure. Recovery of the G-722 submarine continued under the cover story, with hydraulic and seal problems, plutonium contamination from torpedo warheads found, the mission declared finished 9 August via Event 36-A, and later messages on repairs and relocation. The Soviet tug departed, and the team viewed the recovered hulk and torpedo fluid, anticipating a difficult examination.

nodes.title: Glomar cover story and Soviet-shadowed recovery operation at sea
key_items: w a i t i n g
a n x i o u s l y
nodes.summary: The page describes a covert recovery mission in which the HGE ship, under a commercial mining research cover, completed residual tasks such as recovering wave-rider buoys (about $25,000 total) despite Soviet ships nearby. Overt commercial messages on 10 and 11 August stated repair efforts on a nodule collector vehicle and a changed destination near Midway. A Soviet tug left, and the crew believed the cover held. The crew then waited anxiously on deck to glimpse the recovered target.

nodes.title: r e w a r d
nodes.summary: Describes the recovery of a Soviet G-II submarine's contents by the HGE ship (Project AZORIAN). Covers the retrieval of a torpedo-juice Jerry-can from the well, radiation readings, the mission crew's handover at Lahaina Roads, Hawaii, cover arrangements (Summa Ocean Mining, press, messages), and the DCI Colby's advice to the Mission Director. Also covers the operation's six-year timeline, the 1975 media leak, Soviet monitoring, cost-benefit reasoning, and broader benefits to deep-ocean mining and heavy-lift technology.

The section covers the Glomar Explorer (AZORIAN) project from 1972 to 1978: the AZORIAN Review Panel's findings on well-managed but high-risk engineering and cost growth; the 40 Committee's approval and the ship's trials, transit, and conversion; second West Coast trials and Nixon's June 1974 approval of recovering a sunken Soviet submarine; the 1974 recovery under a commercial mining cover; the August 1978 Soviet-shadowed recovery, plutonium contamination, and mission end; and the handover, Colby's advice, the 1975 leak, costs, and wider benefits.

summary: Covers the Glomar Explorer (AZORIAN) project, 1972-1978: AZORIAN Review Panel findings on well-managed but high-risk engineering and cost growth; 40 Committee approval, ship trials, transit and conversion; West Coast trials; Nixon's June 1974 approval to recover a sunken Soviet submarine; the 1974 recovery under a commercial mining cover; the August 1978 Soviet-shadowed recovery, plutonium contamination and mission end; and the handover, Colby's advice, the 1975 leak, costs and wider benefits.
